extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of literature, culture, and gender studies
extracted.subtask_description: A literary and cultural-critique essay (late-19th/early-20th century) about androcentric influences on games, amusements, child-rearing, and public life, arguing normative points about play, sport, and social policy. Useful for readers studying gendered cultural norms and social criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play instinct equality in childhood
rubrics_metrics.description: The play instinct is common to girls and boys alike; early differentiation of play is cultural, not natural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Children naturally enjoy small imitations of real objects (dolls, toy villages, wooden horses, etc.). Forcing girls into perpetual 'maternal' play (continuous baby dolls, tea sets, dollhouses) and discouraging boys from similar play is 'monstrous.' Little children should not be expected to show precocious maternal feelings; play should not be sex-differentiated beginning in infancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid early sex-based narrowing of play
rubrics_metrics.description: We begin in infancy to forcibly differentiate methods of play long before any natural distinction would appear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing girls only dolls and kitchen sets while boys get broader models (boats, railroads, kites, balls) restricts girls' development. Educational practice should avoid confining girls to a narrow 'sphere' and should encourage broad human development through play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Games should develop team-work as a human skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Team-work is not a masculine characteristic but a human social power; games should teach team-work to both sexes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boys gain the educational advantage of team-work by being admitted to collective games; girls are kept within solitary or domestic imitations that do not cultivate team-work. Play in education should be used to develop desired characteristics under non-androcentric canons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate games of chance vs. skill without gender bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Games of chance are human and shared by both sexes; games of skill have been developed by men but women can succeed when allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Women participate in card games, chess, croquet, tennis if trained. Shortcomings in women's participation are attributed to lack of access and masculinization of games rather than innate incapacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize masculine bias in competitive/projectile sports
rubrics_metrics.description: Many games emphasize projectile/competitive impulses (throwing, hitting, hunting) which are culturally masculinized and not necessarily universal human norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ball and sending a projectile are symbolic of masculine impulses to 'scatter' and 'destroy' while feminine impulses tend to 'gather' and 'construct.' Games built around these impulses will naturally appeal more to men; labeling them as 'human' misrepresents their masculine character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not equate sportsmanship with the best preparation for life
rubrics_metrics.description: The cult of sportsmanship and the claim that sports like football 'fit a man for life' are questionable and may obscure other valuable processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valuable modern processes include invention, discovery, industry, honest service, and administration — qualities not necessarily learned on the football field. The Cook-Peary controversy exemplifies how 'sportsmanlike' can overshadow questions of fact and moral judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amusements should educate and ennoble, not merely amuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic expression and the arts should lift, teach, and inspire rather than degrade into cheap amusement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under demand for mere amusement, drama has cheapened (vaudevilles, picture shows). The goal is to reduce excessive masculinization of amusements and bring out broad human interests that men and women can equally enjoy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of masculine monopoly on public amusements
rubrics_metrics.description: Amusements and entertainments have been masculinized; access and content should be broadened for universal human enjoyment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Women’s increased presence at theatres has begun to modify performances. The desirable change is not 'feminization' but decreased masculinization to allow shared human pleasures and expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public health transparency about 'social diseases'
rubrics_metrics.description: Physicians and public health authorities should disseminate information about venereal/social diseases despite prevailing 'sex tabu' and professional secrecy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacteriological advances warrant public instruction; the medical tradition of secrecy (the Hippocratic 'medical secret') and social taboos obstruct necessary public knowledge. Doctors and boards of health should register such diseases as they do other contagious diseases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mainstream publications for public health education
rubrics_metrics.description: Large-circulation domestic magazines may be effective channels to reach conservative and private households with public-health information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The 'Ladies' Home Journal' published clear accounts of social diseases and, despite losing subscribers, performed public service by reaching otherwise unreached audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require medical examination for marriage license
rubrics_metrics.description: Marriage certificates should be accompanied by a medical certificate certifying applicants free from contagious disease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous to physical exams for army/navy enlistment or life insurance, the proposal argues that marriage and parenthood justify similar safeguards to protect prospective spouses and future children; some western states already require this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic restraint and respect for private persons
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters should avoid intrusive, needless publicity that produces nervous distress for private individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text criticizes a reporter who hounded a young bride into a 'highly nervous state' for gossip with no public interest, labeling such inquisitiveness naive brutality. Ethical journalism should weigh privacy and avoid causing intense distress for trivial gossip.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid normalizing indifference to human suffering due to social roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Society should not accept indifference to visible human agony because the sufferer is 'owned' or accompanied by a hired person; intervention should not be inhibited by deference to owners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An anecdote describes a suffering man ignored because aid-givers 'dare not interfere with the Owner.' The critique functions as a moral guideline: do not let class/ownership relations prevent humane aid.
